findings.claim: `_write_file` (lines 366-382) redirects the decoded mutant content straight onto `mutant.file` with `base64 -d > path`, which truncates the target the moment the redirection opens — it is not a write-to-temp-then-rename. If the exec genuinely fails partway (disk full mid-decode, or the connection to the container is lost after the write completed but before the exit code is reported — exactly the case `saffron/gates/core/witness.py` lines 78-85 names as reachable for a container exec and unreachable for `host_mutator`), `_write_file` raises before `source_mutated`'s `try: yield None / finally: undo` block is ever entered (the call at line 418 is outside that block), so no `git checkout HEAD` is attempted. `witness_gate` then reports this as "could not apply" (tree untouched), when the tree may actually be left mutated or corrupted with nothing restoring it — the precise "silent dirty tree" outcome that same docstring says this implementation must not produce.

`_write_file` is called before the `try/finally` that performs the git-checkout undo (the `try:` only opens on the next line, at 419), so a raise out of `_write_file` is not distinguished from a raise that changed nothing. `witness.py`'s own docstring (lines 78-85) names this exact failure mode as the one obligation `host_mutator` cannot reach but a container-exec mutator can — "a container exec that applies the edit and then loses the connection" — and states plainly that `SA-0062`'s mutator, not just the stub, is bound by it. If `_write_file`'s exec reports failure after the write actually landed inside the container (a lost connection, a container OOM-kill mid-script), `witness_gate` sees `applied=False` and reports "could not apply" instead of "could not restore", leaving a mutated file in the tree with no undo ever attempted and no signal that it happened — the "silent dirty tree this gate exists to refuse" that the module's own top-level docstring (worktree.py is the implementation, witness.py lines 35-42 the promise) is supposed to prevent.

`_read_file` returns `runtime.exec_(...).stdout`, which `runtime._call`/`_decode` (runtime.py:111-114) produces via `bytes.decode("utf-8", errors="replace")` — a lossy, one-way substitution of any invalid UTF-8 byte with U+FFFD. `_write_file` then re-encodes that string and overwrites the file (line 418), so any source file containing even one non-UTF-8 byte anywhere (not just at the mutation site) is silently corrupted in the container's tree beyond the declared find/replace before tests run. `saffron/mutation.py`'s sibling implementation deliberately avoids this by staying in raw bytes throughout (its module docstring calls out byte-identical handling as a requirement), and none of the new tests in `tests/test_worktree.py` use anything but plain ASCII fixtures, so this gap is invisible to the suite.

Every `source_mutated` test in this diff (lines 1047-1120) builds its `Mutant.find`/`replace` from plain identifiers and comparisons — never a quote, backtick, `$`, or backslash — despite `_write_file`'s own docstring (saffron/cell/worktree.py:369-374) naming exactly those characters as the reason it base64-encodes rather than shell-quoting the content directly. Replacing the base64 round trip with a naive `printf "%s" "<content>" > <path>` construction passes every existing test unchanged (none of the fixtures' find/replace text would trigger the difference) while corrupting or failing on any real source line containing a quote or `$` — a near-certainty once a spec actually declares a mutant against real code, which is the very next step this change's own scope note anticipates.
